content_of_post_to_comment: Been musing recently on why it can feel so jarring to work with AI and don't think the term "jagged capabilities" quite captures it. When you trust a colleague who is strong in a particular domain, everything beneath that comes for free. What I mean is: there are certain categories of error which a human expert would almost never make. Mathematicians, for example, don't get confused about whether 9.11 or 9.9 is larger. AI has no such guarantees. Nothing comes for free. One minute it can smash out your hardest task in a domain and you think it really understands the core of what you're trying to build. The next moment it's made such a fundamental error you're left staring at the screen recalibrating everything it's ever told you and questioning your life choices. My read of "jagged" is that it describes the shape of ability across skills. I'm saying it's worse than that: there are no guarantees within a skill. And given you don't know where the holes are, this makes trust very expensive. Not because the error rate is high - it might well be lower than a human's - but because not all errors are equal. The category of error matters too. And it's exhausting to have such high levels of constant vigilance. Of course, experts also make basic errors - though usually for mundane reasons like being tired, limitations that don't exist for machines. I wouldn't expect strong humans to repeat the same errors. This is obviously not a complete theory but it gives a good account of some of the frustrations I have working with AI today that I don't think are well-articulated elsewhere.
